awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Bipolar Membrane Applications in Extractive Metallurgy
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the development of a system that converts salty water into concentrated acid and base using only electricity. Acid is widely used in metal refining processes from primary extraction to product finishing across metals including nickel, lithium, rare earths, and steel. However, current acid production and recycling methods are often associated with the generation of hazardous gases that must be managed. The transportation of acids and precursor chemicals adds further logistical complexity and costs to metals processing plants, especially where primary extraction occurs at remote mining sites. Spent acid is often wholly or partially neutralized on site to form salts of calcium, magnesium, sodium, or iron, which can pose environmental risks and space constraints to mine or refinery sites and surrounding ecosystems. Acid procurement and waste management can account for 30% to 80% of operating expenditures in metals leaching processes. This technology may offer a safer, cleaner, and more energy-efficient alternative for metal extraction with no direct emissions or hazardous byproducts. In addition, this technology may enable sustainable domestic supply chains for critical materials.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a bipolar membrane electrodialysis platform for acid and base production. The adoption of bipolar membrane electrodialysis in metallurgy has been limited due to the low concentrations of acid electrodialysis can produce with current technology. Metals leaching typically requires more concentrated acids and bases than in common applications of electrodialysis such as in the beverage or desalination industries. This technology allows for the doubling of acid concentrations versus traditional electrodialysis by optimizing membrane compositions, reactor component sizing, and operational parameters. Unlike conventional acid generation technologies, this approach avoids combustion, phase changes, or hazardous byproducts. The research builds on recent advances in membrane materials and stack design to improve efficiency and durability, allowing for high-throughput operation with minimal downtime. This technology may enable production of concentrated acid and thus, has important applications in metallurgy, where concentrated acids are widely used to extract metals from ores.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The project team evaluated the commercial potential of its electrochemical technology for recycling acids and bases in hydrometallurgical processes. The team completed over 150 interviews with prospective customers, influencers, and recommenders in the space. The original technical motivation was to reduce the cost, waste, and supply chain burden associated with chemical use in critical minerals refining, where large volumes of acids and bases are often purchased, used once, and discarded after neutralization.

 

During the project, the project team conducted customer discovery across the rare earth element (REE), nickel, lithium, EPC, metallurgical processing, and industrial supply chain spaces. These interviews helped the team move beyond technical assumptions and better understand how customers evaluate new process equipment. The team learned that prospective customers care not only about reagent cost, but also about reliability, ease of integration, waste handling, permitting risk, maintenance burden, and whether a new technology can operate within existing plant constraints. Customer discovery produced several clear market takeaways. REE refiners viewed acid and reagent costs as major OpEx drivers and indicated that even a 10% reduction would motivate switching to a new technology. EPC firms said operators strongly influence equipment selection, while EPCs also avoid the risk of recommending unproven systems to customers. Lithium refiners confirmed that acids and reagents are major cost drivers, while sulfuric acid plants can also represent major CapEx and provide valuable energy, especially at remote sites. Nickel refiners emphasized effluent management, especially where evaporation is impractical, suggesting value in salt recovery and turning that into acid and base.

 

The project sharpened the team’s understanding of its initial market and commercialization path. Before customer discovery, the team was considering several possible applications for its platform technology. Through the I-Corps process, the team gained evidence that REE refining is a strong near-term opportunity because customers face severe pain points around chemical procurement, waste management, and domestic supply chain development. The work also helped identify technical metrics that matter to customers, including acid concentration, energy use, membrane lifetime, product consistency, and long duration operation on representative process streams.

 The intellectual merit of this project lies in translating an electrochemical separation technology from a laboratory bench-scale towards a practical industrial application. The customer discovery process helped define which technical questions are most important for commercialization and which performance metrics should guide future research and development. This improved the company’s ability to design experiments, prioritize engineering work, and evaluate whether the technology can meet real industrial needs.

 The broader impacts of the project are tied to cleaner and more resilient domestic materials supply chains. REEs are important for clean energy, electronics, transportation, and national security. Technologies that reduce chemical consumption and waste generation in refining could lower environmental impacts while supporting domestic processing capacity. I-Corps helped identify a more focused path toward that goal by connecting technical development with direct input from potential customers, partners, and industry stakeholders.
